tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
After payments, digital gold, institutional adoption and strategic reserves, what is the next reason for the world to need Bitcoin?

Markets can survive falling prices.

Assets struggle for much longer when they run out of stories.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
But the question facing Bitcoin is no longer whether people have heard of it, whether institutions can access it or whether governments will tolerate it.

Those battles have largely been fought.

The next question is harder.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Two of the world's largest crypto exchanges, Binance and Upbit, currently remain without one and must stop offering trading services in Europe until they secure regulatory approval.

None of this means Bitcoin disappears.

Its supply remains structurally limited.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Then came the idea of Bitcoin as a strategic reserve asset for governments.

That has yet to produce the scale of sovereign demand its supporters expected.

Meanwhile, regulation is becoming real.

The EU's MiCA framework is now fully operational.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Then Bitcoin became "digital gold": an asset that would protect portfolios during periods of economic and geopolitical uncertainty.

That argument looks considerably weaker when Bitcoin falls alongside other risk assets.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text: That has not happened on a meaningful scale. El Salvador became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 and reversed the policy in 2025.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Technology and AI companies are competing for the same risk capital, with the record SpaceX IPO providing one recent example.

But the deeper problem is more uncomfortable.

Bitcoin may be running out of narratives.

It was supposed to become a global payment system.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Bitcoin has also become increasingly correlated with the Nasdaq and S&P 500 as institutional investors entered the market through ETFs.

Capital is simply finding other places to go.

tweets.author: elviseckardtrec.bsky.social
tweets.text:
Bitcoin has lost half its value since October. The more interesting problem is that it may also be running out of reasons to own it.

Around $8.5 billion has flowed out of US Bitcoin ETFs in just two months. Institutional demand has been weakening since September.
